posts.text: tl:dr if society’s wealth is increasingly bound up in ownership of capital, that is a policy issue that ought to be addressed through tax policy but it doesn’t reflect *personal culpability* of individual rich people for having some combination of smarts and good luck

It’s also not the case that harmful business activities are particularly associated with billionaire wealth.

The alcohol industry is very damaging, does a lot of bad lobbying to prevent harm reduction, and is not associated with famous billionaires.

slowboring.com/p/booze-tax

Here, again, I just think we should be addressing the main issues — the structure of tax policy, the distribution of consumption opportunities, etc — not moralizing around edge cases. 

There are net harmful successful businesses but that’s extremely rare.

But conversely, while there is nothing wrong with building a great business and becoming extraordinarily wealthy there *is* something wrong with hoarding that wealthy for personal consumption or to pass to your kids.

slowboring.com/p/the-real-pr…

I am prepared to defend the founders and investors as mostly (not 100% but well over 50%) people engaged in largely pro-social activity, but I think it’s worth really engaging with the main case rather than focusing on Taylor Swift. 

slowboring.com/p/lets-all-pr…

I think it’s interesting that going back at least as far as Nozick and Wilt Chamberlain the go-to examples for this argument are always celebrity entertainers when obviously the vast majority of extreme wealth is either successful founders, successful investors, or their heirs.
